clue.text: This brewing by the weird - sisters?

definitions.text: This brewing by the weird - sisters?

blocks.clueFragment: This brewing by the weird - sisters?
blocks.note: surface: some odd sisters making tea or beer
setter's reading: the three witches in Macbeth, whose cauldron chant is 'Double, double toil and ...'

explanation.surface: Three strange sisters are cooking something up together.
explanation.walkthrough: The Weird Sisters are the witches of Macbeth; their chant over the cauldron runs 'Double, double toil and trouble'. TROUBLE is what they are brewing.
explanation.definitionFit: To brew trouble is an idiom for stirring up mischief, and the witches literally do so in their spell.

clue.text: Designer's guides recently among temporary staff

indicators.note: among means in the midst of, so one word sits inside the other

blocks.note: temps are temporary office workers
late can mean recently, as in 'of late'

explanation.surface: Fashion guidance has lately been passed round the agency workers.
explanation.definitionFit: Templates are patterns or shaped guides used by designers and craftsmen to reproduce a form.

clue.text: Order banished by St Patrick

blocks.note: surface: a religious order expelled by the saint
setter's reading: a zoological order, the snakes Patrick is said to have driven from Ireland

explanation.surface: Ireland's patron saint drives out a religious brotherhood.
explanation.walkthrough: Legend says St Patrick drove all the snakes out of Ireland; the order is the biological rank, not a monastic one.
explanation.definitionFit: Ophidia is an old scientific name for the order of reptiles comprising snakes.

clue.text: This metal from an old Roman province

blocks.note: first meaning: a pewter-like alloy of tin, antimony and copper
second meaning: the Latin name for the province of Britain

explanation.walkthrough: 'from' joins the two meanings; the surface makes the metal sound mined in that province.
explanation.definitionFit: Britannia metal is a silvery tableware alloy, and Britannia was the Roman name for their British province.

clue.text: Every oriental has an honour

blocks.note: E for eastern
the indefinite article
CH, Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: All eastern people are said to hold a title of distinction.
explanation.walkthrough: CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: Each and every both pick out all members of a group taken individually.

clue.text: One - needs two to make a century

definitions.text: One - needs two to make a century

blocks.clueFragment: One - needs two to make a century
blocks.note: surface: a cricketer needs a partner to reach a hundred runs

blocks.clueFragment: needs two to make a century
blocks.note: setter's reading: the figure 1 followed by two zeros writes the number 100

explanation.surface: A batsman cannot reach a hundred runs without help from a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: A century is a hundred, written as the digit 1 followed by two zeros, which are noughts.
explanation.definitionFit: Noughts are zeros, and placing two of them after the digit 1 writes the number one hundred.

clue.text: Deals successfully with poor Otis (age ten)

indicators.note: something poor is in a bad state, so its letters come out in a broken order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone handles a ten-year-old boy called Otis with skill.
explanation.definitionFit: To negotiate an obstacle is to get past it, so the verb also means to cope with something successfully.

clue.text: A French trick to get clear of tackle

blocks.note: the French for a
to rig is to fix dishonestly, a trick

explanation.surface: A Frenchman uses a ruse to escape being tackled in a match.
explanation.walkthrough: Tackle here is a ship's rigging, not a rugby challenge.
explanation.definitionFit: To unrig a vessel is to strip it of its rigging, the ropes and gear called tackle.

clue.text: One that binds about capital cover

definitions.text: One that binds about capital cover

blocks.clueFragment: One that binds about capital cover
blocks.note: surface: a bookbinder at work on a cover
setter's reading: capital as the head, so a covering for the head

explanation.surface: A bookbinder works around the cover of a grand volume.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital comes from Latin caput, head; a ribbon binds round the crown of what sits on it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hatband is a strip of ribbon or fabric fastened round the crown of a hat.

clue.text: Rope made of bed-clothes? Only one

definitions.text: Rope made of bed-clothes? Only one

blocks.note: surface: an escape rope knotted from bed linen
setter's reading: on a sailing boat the rope that trims a sail has a name that is also a single piece of bedding

explanation.surface: A prisoner ties bedding together to climb out of a window.
explanation.walkthrough: On a sailing boat the sheet is the rope controlling a sail; one sheet is also one bed-cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheet is both a sailing rope attached to a sail's corner and a single piece of bed linen.

clue.text: Muslim leader had 1 ac in the half-mile

indicators.note: 1 across is TROUBLE, and letters in trouble are thrown into disorder
in places the jumbled word inside the other piece

blocks.note: the first half of the word mile
the word had, jumbled

explanation.surface: A Muslim leader had a spot of bother during a half-mile race.
explanation.walkthrough: '1 ac' is the cross-reference to 1 across, TROUBLE, used here as the anagram signal: had in trouble. Put that inside MI to get MAHDI.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mahdi is the prophesied redeemer of Islam, a title claimed by the Sudanese leader who fought Gordon at Khartoum.

clue.text: Smoke that French female out of Riga's ruins

indicators.note: something in ruins has been knocked apart, so these letters lie in a new order
one piece stands outside the other, wrapping round it

blocks.note: the French word for 'that', feminine form
the letters of Riga, rearranged

explanation.surface: A French woman smokes amid the ruins of the Latvian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: CETTE is French 'that' before a feminine noun; the jumbled RIGA goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A cigarette is a common kind of smoke, the noun sense of something one smokes.

clue.text: Was this the mode of Miss Languish?

definitions.text: Was this the mode of Miss Languish?

blocks.clueFragment: Was this the mode of Miss Languish?
blocks.note: surface: a question about a lady's fashion or manner
setter's reading: a musical mode that sounds like the heroine's first name with an extra letter

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what style or fashion a certain young lady followed.
explanation.walkthrough: Lydia Languish is the romantic heroine of Sheridan's play The Rivals; the Lydian mode is one of the ancient Greek musical scales, so her first name almost spells it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lydian is the name of a musical mode, a scale from ancient Greek and church music.

clue.text: Label Nan in a way as sluggish

indicators.note: in places the two words inside the abbreviation for a road

blocks.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
a tag is a label
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tags a grandmother as slow-moving.
explanation.definitionFit: Stagnant water does not flow, and figuratively a stagnant economy or person is slow and inactive.

clue.text: Explain about Brown being a man of money

indicators.note: about can mean turned around, so the colour word's letters are moved

blocks.note: to account for is to explain
tan is a brown colour

explanation.surface: Someone describes a man named Brown who is rich.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown reads like a surname, but it is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: An accountant manages and audits finances professionally, so is a man whose work is money.

clue.text: Coach of coaches?

blocks.note: first meaning: to instruct or drill
second meaning: a line of railway carriages hauled together

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a sports trainer of trainers; really one word is the verb coach and also a string of railway coaches.
explanation.definitionFit: To train someone is to coach them, and a train is a set of linked carriages.

clue.text: Statesman, poet and scholar divided by a point

indicators.note: the two people are split apart with something set between them

blocks.note: John Clare, the English nature poet
north, a compass point
a don is a university teacher

explanation.surface: A list of distinguished figures with a compass point between two of them.
explanation.walkthrough: John Clare was a 19th-century English poet; a don is an Oxford or Cambridge academic.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, was Lord Chancellor and chief minister to Charles II, a celebrated English statesman.

clue.text: Fateful Church of England Order, serving its purpose

indicators.note: to order things is to arrange them, here into a new sequence

blocks.note: taken as written
CE is the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A momentous decree from the Anglican Church fulfils its aim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like a church command, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Effectual means producing the intended result, so it describes something that does its job.

clue.text: Youthful bloom lost by Echo

blocks.note: surface: someone named Echo losing her youthful looks
setter's reading: the beautiful youth of Greek myth whom the nymph Echo loved and lost, turned into a flower

explanation.surface: A woman called Echo has lost the bloom of her youth.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth the nymph Echo pined for a beautiful youth who loved only his reflection; he died and became the flower that bears his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Narcissus is both the mythical youth Echo loved and the daffodil genus of spring flowers.

clue.text: Mince-pie with sarong in SE Asia

indicators.note: mincing chops something into small bits, so the letters are cut up and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Christmas pastry eaten by someone wearing a wrap skirt in the tropics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mince-pie' looks like a single festive dish, but Mince is the anagram signal working on pie and sarong.
explanation.definitionFit: Singapore is a city-state at the tip of the Malay peninsula, so it is a place found in SE Asia.

clue.text: They have eyes for sewers, if not for DJs

definitions.text: They have eyes for sewers, if not for DJs

blocks.note: surface: someone fond of drains
setter's reading: people who sew use the eyed sort; record players use a stylus of the same name without one

explanation.surface: Something keeps watch over drains but not over disc jockeys.
explanation.walkthrough: Sewers are people who sew, not drains; a gramophone stylus is also called a needle, and has no eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Needles have an eye for thread, and the stylus that plays a record is also called a needle.

clue.text: Was Miss Malone's killer the scarlet kind ?

definitions.text: Was Miss Malone's killer the scarlet kind ?

blocks.clueFragment: Was Miss Malone's killer the scarlet kind ?
blocks.note: surface: a murder mystery about a woman and a red-handed killer
setter's reading: the Dublin song of Molly Malone

explanation.surface: A detective asks whether a lady's murderer was a scarlet-clad villain.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Irish song Molly Malone, the fishmonger 'died of a fever, and no one could save her'; scarlet fever is one sort of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A fever is an illness with raised temperature, and scarlet fever is a named infectious kind.

clue.text: Stoker's flier was one

blocks.note: surface: a boiler-room stoker's pigeon or aeroplane
setter's reading: Bram Stoker, author of Dracula, whose count flies as a bat

explanation.surface: A fireman's pet bird or plane belonged to some type.
explanation.walkthrough: Bram Stoker wrote Dracula; the count can take bat form, and the creature he is also gives its name to a bat.
explanation.definitionFit: Count Dracula is the archetypal vampire, an undead creature that drinks blood.

clue.text: Protestant leader on the throne is full of ideas

indicators.note: the leader is the one at the front, so only the opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: the first letter of Protestant
regnant means reigning, as a monarch on the throne

explanation.surface: A Protestant ruler who has taken the crown is bursting with plans.
explanation.definitionFit: Pregnant can mean figuratively full of meaning or ideas, as in a pregnant pause or a pregnant mind.

clue.text: Summons may be yellow

blocks.note: first meaning: calls someone over a loudspeaker or bleeper
second meaning: leaves of a book, which in the telephone directory of businesses are yellow

explanation.walkthrough: Yellow Pages is the classified business telephone directory, printed on yellow paper.
explanation.definitionFit: To page someone is to summon them, and leaves of a book are pages, as in the Yellow Pages directory.

clue.text: Sound cohesion back at last

indicators.note: at last points to the closing stretch of the word that follows
back means read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: the final five letters of cohesion

explanation.surface: A sound sticking-together returns in the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A noise is a sound, especially a loud or unwanted one.

clue.text: One quiet Scot's returned to the course

indicators.note: returned means going back the way it came, so the string is read from the end

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
p, piano, is the musical mark for quiet
Mac is a typical Scot, with the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: A lone, silent Scotsman goes back to the golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: The course is a course of a meal, not a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: Scampi, deep-fried langoustine tails, are served as one course of a meal, a dish.

clue.text: Check ship's front timber

blocks.note: first meaning: to stop or hold back a flow
second meaning: the upright timber at a vessel's bow

explanation.walkthrough: One word is the verb for halting a flow and also the bow timber of a wooden ship.
explanation.definitionFit: To stem bleeding is to check it, and a stem is the upright post forming a ship's prow.

clue.text: Gad about like the army MP about tea-time

indicators.note: about means going round, so the first piece wraps round the time

blocks.note: in the Commons a member who is a military officer is styled 'the honourable and gallant member'
four o'clock, written in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone flits around like a soldier politician at four in the afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: In Parliament an officer MP was once addressed as 'the honourable and gallant member'; four o'clock is the traditional British tea-time.
explanation.definitionFit: To gallivant is to roam about in search of pleasure, which is what to gad about means.

clue.text: One's electrical consumption

blocks.note: a unit is a single one
the possessive ending kept as its letter

explanation.surface: A household's electricity use, as shown on the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: A British electricity bill counts consumption in units, each one a kilowatt-hour.
explanation.definitionFit: Electricity used is metered and billed in units, so the units are the measure of consumption.

clue.text: Doubt he did it?

blocks.note: first meaning: to mistrust or have misgivings about
second meaning: a person thought to be guilty of a crime

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence of doubt; really the verb and the noun of one word stand side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: To suspect is to mistrust, and a suspect is the person police believe may have committed a crime.

clue.text: Hammers and pounds in reactive power source

indicators.note: in sets one piece inside the other before they are stirred
a reactive substance changes readily, so the letters undergo change

blocks.note: l is the abbreviation for a pound, doubled for the plural
steam drove engines in the industrial age

explanation.surface: Tools and money tied up in a nuclear reactor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hammers and pounds' looks like a pair of verbs; pounds is the money.
explanation.definitionFit: Mallets are hammers, usually with heads of wood or rubber.
